item.title: LSU is ready to party: Lane Kiffin’s debut brings fireworks to Death Valley after revival-like buildup
item.description: Lane Kiffin's LSU debut against Clemson has Death Valley buzzing with celebrities, tailgaters, and a Mardi Gras-like atmosphere in Baton Rouge.
item.content:encoded:
Lane Kiffin’s highly anticipated debut as LSU’s head coach created a seismic shift around a campus that already knows how to throw a party.

What had been missing?

Well, it doesn’t take a rocket scientist to understand the financial benefits Kiffin’s arrival has created in Baton Rouge.

LANE KIFFIN KNOWS THERE AREN’T EXCUSES AT LSU. NOW COMES THE TEST OF MAKING IT WORTH THE PRICE OF ADMISSION

Add some spice to the jambalaya brewing outside Tiger Stadium, where tailgaters were preparing for a Mardi Gras-like atmosphere, and you have a time bomb ready to explode along the Bayou.

The community couldn’t have asked for anything better, especially with the apathy that had set in under Brian Kelly before he was ultimately fired.

There is also a new band in town running the show, which starts at the top with Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry.

It's LSU against the world, and the past few weeks have made that crystal clear.

INSIDE A LOUISIANA COURTROOM': SEC-LSU LEGAL CIRCUS PLAYED OUT LIKE A JOHN GRISHAM NOVEL IN STUNNING SHOWDOWN

Whether it's the never-ending topic of the Tigers administration signing off on bringing in former professional athletes to play college football or basketball, or the palpable sense of excitement around football in this part of the country, the energy is undeniable.

"I got down here two days ago, with coolers filled with cold beer and the grill prepared to flame up some Alligator," Thomas from the New Orleans area told OutKick. He's (Kiffin) brought a new sense of excitement to LSU football, even though we don't take a back seat to anyone.

"This is f---ing LSU, it's time to start competing for titles again."

Well, Thomas isn’t lying, there is obviously a sense of excitement around Baton Rouge that I personally haven’t seen in a few years. And don't forget, this fanbase is spread out all over the state and Gulf Coast, with Tiger blood running deep into family traditions.

The party atmosphere only picked up as night fell, with fans of both LSU and Clemson going at each other around the local watering holes and local restaurants.

Sure, there have been distractions around the LSU football program tied to the rostering of former professional athletes who had sued the SEC, but none of that will matter once the ball is finally kicked off tonight.

JUDGE GRANTS INJUNCTION AGAINST NCAA, SEC, ALLOWING ATHLETES WITH NFL TIES ELIGIBLE TO PLAY FOR LSU, OTHERS

In what will remind folks of Deion Sanders' first season at Colorado, the celebrities will be out tonight.

From congressional leaders, musical acts to even singer Lainey Wilson, everyone was headed to Baton Rouge for the party that will take place under the lights tonight in Death Valley.

And, rightfully so. There will be no bigger party in the South than what we will witness inside Tiger Stadium. After leaving Ole Miss before their run in the College Football Playoff, all eyes have been fixated on LSU.

There will be a large group of college football fans that want to Dabo Swinney lead his Clemson Tigers into town and pul off the upset. For that, I can’t fault the folks who will actually cheer on Swinney, even though he's also on the list of unlikeable coaches from a fans perspective.

LSU MIGHT HAVE TO SUE THE SEC IF THIS LEGAL WAR IS EXPEDITED, WHILE DABO SWINNEY IS STAYING IN HIS 'LANE'

But, that's where we are at, with plenty of people wanting to see Lane Kiffin fail at LSU. Though, I'd imagine the SEC is still wanting the Tigers to thrive, even with the ongoing lawsuits being filed by multiple parties pertaining to pro-athletes returning to college.

Make no mistake about it, Lane Kiffin is the biggest story in college football. It's not Curt Cignetti or what's taking place at other schools around the sport.

No, for the past seven months, the most discussed topic in college athletics has been what's transpiring in Baton Rouge, and by proxy Ole Miss.

For that, there's a strong sense of urgency around these parts. LSU fans are not in the mood to hear the world 'patience', especially with the amount of money being spent on the football program to win immediately.

Is that fair for Lane Kiffin? Probably not, but welcome to the new era of college athletics under the guise of NIL and revenue-sharing.

As I made my way around campus on Friday afternoon, the drinking had already begun and the grills were already lit.

It's on Kiffin and the football program to deliver the party favors tonight, with a whole bunch of public perception at stake.

Welcome to the show, with plenty of fireworks already being ignited over the past seven months.

item.title: The marriage warning sign that may be worse than fighting — and 4 ways to turn things around
item.description: From flirting and dating to spending quality time without phones, experts share how small daily gestures can reverse quiet quitting in a marriage.
item.content:encoded:
Much like the workplace term that means doing the bare minimum, "quiet quitting" could also happen in marriage, sometimes gradually.

The informal term — which is not a clinical diagnosis — refers to spouses who remain together while reducing their emotional effort, communication or involvement in the relationship, according to experts.

New York City divorce lawyer James Sexton described what "quiet quitting" can look like at home and at work: "I'm not going to go through the dramatic gesture of ending this thing. I'm just going to stop. I'm going to stop paying attention. I'm going to stop participating."

‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT

Silently pulling away from the relationship may seem to be easier than going through the "trauma" of divorce, Sexton told Fox News Digital — and the person avoids looking like the "bad guy" for ending the relationship.

"Very often, you actually receive more sympathy because you're perceived as the victim of the breakup as opposed to the perpetrator," he added.

A lack of effort in a relationship can be a bigger warning sign than frequent conflict, according to Sexton.

"When people are fighting, it kind of means there’s still skin in the game," he said. "The opposite of love is not hate … it’s indifference."

NEARLY 1 IN 3 MARRIED AMERICANS AREN'T HAVING SEX — EXPERT REVEALS HOW TO BRING BACK THE SPARK

Dr. Mindy DeSeta, a clinical sexologist and licensed mental health counselor in Miami, said some couples seek help after about 30 years of marriage, when the demands of family life have eased.

"The kids are gone, or they're hitting that retirement age, so they don't have the life distractions, and they're realizing, ‘Wow. I actually quiet quit my relationship when my kids were toddlers,’" she told Fox News Digital.

DeSeta identified four relationship principles, including the following.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Couples experiencing quiet quitting may continue to function well as a team, managing the household and other responsibilities while becoming emotionally disconnected.

DeSeta said this disconnection can develop gradually, as spouses begin living increasingly separate lives.

"When you stop spending the evenings together … you each are kind of doing your own thing. Your shows are different. You're going to bed at different times … You may have different friend groups. You're working out at different times," she listed.

Both experts shared tips for addressing emotional disconnection between romantic partners.

Reconnection often requires small, active steps that re-start the momentum, rather than making grand gestures, Sexton suggested.

The divorce lawyer encouraged re-visiting the simple acts and gestures that both partners enjoyed early in the relationship.

His suggestions included sending sweet "good morning" texts, writing a note complimenting a partner, or sharing a song that sparked a romantic memory.

"It costs nothing, takes 30 seconds to do it," he said. "What does it cost to write an email with a list of 10 things I like about you? These are not only things we welcome receiving under any circumstances, but they're actually reminders."

Oftentimes, quiet quitting looks like zoning out during moments of quality time, DeSeta said.

If one partner scrolls on a phone while watching a movie together, the device can become "the third member of the relationship," signaling where that partner’s attention lies, the expert cautioned.

"When you're on your phone, you're actually saying, ‘I'm choosing to do this versus spending quality time with you,'" she added.

In addition to paying attention during one-on-one activities, the act of asking personal questions — as simple as "how was your day?" — can also help to restore a connection, DeSeta said.

Instead of leading with a complaint about the relationship, Sexton suggested using a positive approach.

For example, instead of saying, "We never spend time with each other anymore," try calling back a positive memory and suggest recreating it.

"Focusing on what we need to work on is harder than focusing on what it is that we really like about this person, what drew us to them to begin with," he said. "Chances are, they might feel far away from who they were at the beginning of the relationship."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"And maybe our job in a relationship is to try to remind each other of the 'you' and the 'me' before we became the 'we.'"

Making an active effort to flirt with a partner can boost mood while signaling continued romantic interest, according to DeSeta.

"Let your partner know that you are there to earn them every day," she said, emphasizing the importance of continuing to learn about and pursue a partner throughout the relationship.

"Let them know in the most subtle ways every single day that you care about them, that you're thinking about them – and if you do that, you kind of break this cycle of the quiet quitting and eventually it starts coming back to you."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Sexton reminded couples that their time together is limited, so illness or tragedy should not be the catalyst for renewed effort.

"Every single person in your life is not permanently gifted to you — they're loaned," he said. "There’s a finite number of times that you're going to be with this person, see this person, tell this person that you love them."

item.title: Ex-Fetterman staffers promise more damaging details after blistering report: ‘Tip of the iceberg’
item.description: Former staffers for John Fetterman launched an X account promising damaging revelations well beyond the Wall Street Journal report.
item.content:encoded:
In just over a week, former staffers for John Fetterman, D-Pa., are planning to go public with inside details after expressing what they called disgust at his work as a legislator.

"We’re a group of former campaign & Senate staffers for John Fetterman who are disgusted with what he's become. If you were troubled by yesterday's Wall Street Journal story... trust us, that's just the tip of the iceberg," the group wrote in a post to X.

"It’s even worse than you thought."

The new social media account, which is calling itself "Former Fetterman Staffers" (FFS) alleges it will reveal additional unflattering details of the embattled senator’s office as he also faces blowback over Wall Street Journal reporting chronicling his reluctance to engage in the basic duties of his office.

FETTERMAN FACES DEM REVOLT AS BOMBSHELL REPORT FUELS PUSH TO OUST HIM: 'DISGRACE'

The FFS acronym notoriously also stands for "for f---s sake."

Fetterman routinely blew off constituent meetings, neglected legislative review and declined to make in-state public appearances, according to a Wall Street Journal report published on Thursday, drawing immediate backlash online.

"There is a lot I could say about this report of John Fetterman’s pathetic behavior as a senator," Rep. Chris Deluzio, D-Pa., said on X. "But between the laziness, disrespect, and willingness to carry water for a foreign government, it shows us something we already know: this man has no sense of duty."

"John Fetterman is a disgrace," Rep. Brendan Boyle, D-Pa., said in a post of his own. "Our state deserves better than a lazy trust fund baby who is too lazy to do the job."

Pennsylvania state Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta, who is the vice chair of the Democratic National Committee, also condemned Fetterman’s behavior.

"This report is horrifying, but not new to many of us in PA. John barely showed up as [Lieutenant Governor] and is constantly MIA as our senator," Kenyatta wrote.

"When he’s not on FOX cheerleading Trump & endless wars, he is attacking the very neighbors who gave him a chance. 2028 can’t come soon enough," he continued.

DNC VICE CHAIR ATTACKS DEMOCRATIC SEN. JOHN FETTERMAN: 'YOU’RE A MESS'

Conor Lamb, a former Pennsylvania congressman who ran against Fetterman in the 2022 primary for the party’s nomination, called on Fetterman to resign.

"John, if there is a decent bone left in your body, just quit. It’s an insult to decent people in our state for you to treat them and the office this way," Lamb wrote, referring to an instance where Fetterman blew off a meeting with paralyzed military veterans.

As reactions continue to pour in, Former Fetterman Staffers, the new group on X, told viewers that they would set a deadline for some of its upcoming revelations.

"Set your calendar for September 14th -- the day the Senate is back in session -- for our first drop. (Let's be honest, maybe the 15th: he'll skip Monday's votes)," the group said.

Despite raising questions and rage towards Fetterman, some observers condemned the staffers for what they called a lack of loyalty.

"So disloyal. He gave you jobs and opportunities and advanced your careers, and you publicly turn on him and set up an X account to attack him?" Marc Thiessen, a political pundit and former White House speechwriter for the Bush Administration, wrote on X.

"Honorable thing, if you disagree, is to resign quietly and work for someone else you prefer. You are pathetic," he continued.

Mark Morgan, political director for the Republican Governors Association, echoed Thiessen's thinking, blasting the group for its anonymity.

"Staff rule #1: it's not about you Staff rule #2: Your boss had the courage to put their name on a ballot. If you've chosen to become a click-seeking bottom feeder, at least have the courage to put your own name on it," Morgan said.

EMBATTLED REP TONY GONZALES ANNOUNCES PLANS TO RESIGN AMID SEXUAL MISCONDUCT ALLEGATIONS

"I’m disgusted by anonymous leakers, actually," Harmeet Dhillon, Trump's assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division at the U.S. Department of Justice, also chimed in.

Fetterman’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

item.title: NJ mayor demands sanctuary policy rollback after baby killed in crash allegedly involving illegal immigrant
item.description: Jackson Township's mayor says New Jersey's Immigrant Trust Directive must be rolled back after an unlicensed illegal immigrant allegedly killed a baby.
item.content:encoded:
The mayor of the New Jersey township where a baby boy was killed last week after an illegal immigrant allegedly struck the child's family with her car in a grocery store parking lot told Fox News Digital that the state's sanctuary policies should be rolled back to help prevent similar tragedies.

"If our police pull somebody over and they're undocumented... they can't call the federal agencies, they can't call ICE. That needs to change," Jennifer Kuhn, the mayor of Jackson Township, said in an interview on Thursday. "Condolences at this point are not enough. At this point, leadership needs to step in. And we have to do something."

Authorities say Maria Cobon-Guzman, a Guatemalan national who did not have a driver's license, hit a mother pushing a stroller carrying her 9-month-old son and 5-year-old daughter in the parking lot of a kosher grocery store in Jackson on Aug. 28. The infant died, while the mother and 5-year-old were critically injured.

Kuhn argued the crash underscores the need to scrap New Jersey policies that, in most cases, limit cooperation between local, county and state law enforcement and federal immigration authorities.

ILLEGAL ALIEN'S ‘INEXCUSABLE’ CRIME SPARKS INTERSTATE CLASH BETWEEN GOP SEN, DEM GOV: ‘YOU SHOULD BE ASHAMED’

"These issues shouldn't happen whether you're illegal or legal. But the problem is that we can't hold them accountable if they're not documented and they're illegal aliens," she added.

Cobon-Guzman, 20, was charged with manslaughter. Prosecutors also charged Ariadna Lazaro-Flores, alleging she allowed Cobon-Guzman to drive her vehicle despite knowing she did not have a driver's license.

Lazaro-Flores, an illegal immigrant from Mexico, was charged with endangering the welfare of an incompetent person, according to an inmate report.

Both women illegally entered the U.S. during the Biden administration, with Lazaro-Flores doing so five times in October 2023 and being removed each time, the Department of Homeland Security previously told Fox News Digital.

Cobon-Guzman entered once in October 2023 but was released unvetted into the nation’s interior, DHS added. On July 31, an immigration judge issued an order of removal against her.

DEADLY ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT TRUCK CRASH EXPOSED FAILURES ON THE ROAD AND AT THE BORDER: KEY SENATOR

At the center of Kuhn's criticism is New Jersey's Immigrant Trust Directive, a policy implemented under former Gov. Phil Murphy in 2018.

Among other provisions, the directive generally prohibits police from asking about a person's immigration status, notifying U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) when someone is being released from custody, or sharing certain non-public personal information for civil immigration enforcement purposes.

Current New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed legislation codifying the directive into state law in March. She also signed an executive order in February that prohibits ICE agents from using nonpublic areas of state property to stage or conduct operations unless they have a judicial warrant.

NJ TAXPAYERS ON THE HOOK FOR $12M MORE AS DEM GOVERNOR PROTECTS ILLEGAL ALIENS BATTLING DEPORTATION

Kuhn is calling for the Jackson Township Council to pass a resolution demanding an end to such policies at the state level.

"I know that there's other towns around in Ocean County and in other counties that are also doing the same. Something needs to change," Kuhn said.

Supporters of the policies say they help build trust between immigrant communities and local law enforcement by encouraging victims and witnesses to report crimes without fear that routine interactions with police will lead to scrutiny over their immigration status.

Dan Prochilo, a spokesperson for the New Jersey Attorney General's Office, defended the Immigrant Trust Directive and other sanctuary-style reforms signed by Sherrill.

County jails and state prisons can notify ICE when someone is being released if they are charged with or have been convicted of certain violent or serious crimes, Prochilo said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

Some of those crimes include assault, stalking, criminal sexual contact, arson and burglary, according to the Immigrant Trust Directive.

New Jersey jails can also notify ICE if a suspect has been convicted of a felony within the past five years or is under a final deportation order from a federal immigration judge, Prochilo said.

"Such notice has been provided regularly in appropriate cases by New Jersey law enforcement agencies since the Immigrant Trust Directive took effect in 2019," Prochilo added.

Fox News Digital also reached out to Sherrill's office for comment.

item.title: Patrick Clancy speaks out after hung jury in Lindsay Clancy case, addresses prospect of another trial
item.description: Patrick Clancy says enduring another trial would be "extraordinarily painful" after a hung jury led to a mistrial in Lindsay Clancy's murder case.
item.content:encoded:
Patrick Clancy broke his silence after a mistrial was declared in Lindsay Clancy’s case, saying the prospect of enduring another trial over the killings of their three children is "extraordinarily painful."

"Patrick Clancy is grateful to the Court and to the jurors for their hard work, their commitment, and their perseverance. The loss of Patrick’s children is something from which he will never recover and from which there will never be closure," his attorney, David Meier, wrote in a statement issued on Patrick's behalf.

"The prospect of reliving this tragedy through another trial is extraordinarily painful — for Patrick, for his family, and for all us," the statement concluded.

Patrick Clancy has previously asked the public to forgive his ex-wife, who has admitted killing their three children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan. Her attorneys have argued she was legally insane due to postpartum psychosis.

LINDSAY CLANCY'S EX-HUSBAND HAS QUIETLY REMARRIED AND STARTED OVER AMID HER MURDER TRIAL

During the trial, Patrick Clancy testified about the day of the killings on Jan. 24, 2023. The children were killed while he was running errands that included picking up children's stool softener at a CVS store and takeout for dinner. They spoke on the phone while he was out.

On Friday afternoon, Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial in the high-profile murder case after jurors said they were unable to reach a unanimous verdict. It will now be up to prosecutors whether Clancy will be tried again.

The jury spent a week deliberating at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, where supporters and onlookers gathered outside for days awaiting a possible verdict.

The mistrial followed an alleged 11-1 divide among jurors, with Clancy’s defense arguing that the lone holdout juror had acknowledged doubt but was refusing to properly apply the court’s instructions on reasonable doubt.

LINDSAY CLANCY’S EX-HUSBAND DETAILS ‘BIG SPIRAL’ AS EXPERT SAYS ONE PART ‘SCARED ME’ IN MOM’S MURDER TRIAL

The alleged holdout is believed to be one of the three male jurors. Defense attorney Kevin Reddington repeatedly referred to the unnamed juror as a male inside and outside court.

Clancy’s attorneys made an emergency appeal to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court in an attempt to stay the mistrial and force further inquiry into the juror.

Justice Dalila Argaez Wendlandt denied the request Friday afternoon, and shortly after, Sullivan declared a mistrial.

Sullivan said he wants the case retried "sooner rather than later,", suggesting a new trial could potentially take place later this fall. Clancy is due back in court Sept. 29 for a status hearing, trial assignment and a defense Rule 25 motion.

item.title: Before McDonald's and Starbucks, Americans packed these once-beloved lunch counters
item.description: Luncheonettes gave women a place to eat during the workday and thrived during Prohibition, but America's fast food and car culture have reshaped dining habits.
item.content:encoded:
Long before fast-food counters and coffee shops became fixtures of American life, luncheonettes gave generations of Americans an inexpensive place to grab a meal — and helped change where women could eat, work and socialize in public.

The casual restaurants serving simple, inexpensive meals, typically at a lunch counter, began emerging in the late 19th century. They boomed during the 1910s and 1920s and remained popular through the mid-20th century.

Woolworth's, S.H. Kress, S.S. Kresge, Walgreens and Liggett's were among the best-known names associated with lunch counters and luncheonettes in five-and-dime stores, drugstores and other retail establishments.

THE 24-HOUR AMERICAN DINER IS VANISHING — HERE'S WHAT'S DRIVING THE DECLINE

Luncheonettes flourished as Americans increasingly moved into cities and paid employment, said Megan Elias, a curator of food and wine history at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History.

"They fit well with a society that was urbanizing and increasingly organized around paid employment rather than family farms," Elias told Fox News Digital. "Luncheonettes offered food that was affordable and predictable with the kinds of starches and fats people often find comforting."

Their menus typically featured straightforward fare, including roast meats, soups, sandwiches and regional dishes such as baked beans.

But luncheonettes offered more than inexpensive food.

WHY RESTAURANT SERVERS CLEAR YOUR PLATE BEFORE EVERYONE FINISHES EATING

"Luncheonettes were affordable, and because they were associated with daytime, they had an atmosphere of respectability," Elias said. 

"Women and children, who were not generally welcomed in saloons or the dining rooms of men's clubs, could feel comfortable in luncheonettes."

They also gave women in the workforce a place to eat during the day, New York-based culinary historian Linda Pelaccio told Fox News Digital.

Prohibition and World War II further fueled their popularity as soda fountains and luncheonettes became social gathering places and more Americans sought inexpensive meals away from home.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"They were popular in American society because they were quick and less expensive," Pelaccio said. "You could get a lunch and a cup of coffee … and be on your way."

But the same social changes that helped create the luncheonette eventually contributed to its decline.

As jobs shifted to suburban office parks, getting lunch increasingly meant driving, helping fuel the rise of fast-food and drive-thru restaurants, Elias said. Americans' tastes also expanded beyond the traditional luncheonette menu.

"[The luncheonette's decline] is a story of the diversification of the American diet, of increased comfort with foods from many different cultures," Elias said. "It's the story of a shift to car culture rather than walking to lunch."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Malls, struggling downtowns, suburban life and a changing workforce further contributed to the luncheonette's disappearance, Andrew P. Haley, associate professor of American cultural history at the University of Southern Mississippi, told Fox News Digital.

"A big part was the change in women's roles," Haley said. 

"In the 1970s, more and more women worked. Sure, they might go to Woolworth's for lunch, but unlike when they were shopping downtown and needed a place to take a break, they now could take a lunch to work — and often choose healthier foods, diet food and less expensive foods."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Yet for those who remember them, luncheonettes can still evoke something increasingly difficult to find, Elias said, because "sitting shoulder to shoulder with strangers at the lunch counter created a sense of community."

Haley is less convinced that people are nostalgic for actual luncheonettes rather than for an idealized version of such establishments.

"Nostalgic decor might allow us to imagine for an instant that we are regaining community gathering spaces, but the pre-existing community ties that made those spaces collective is no longer there," Haley said.

item.title: The freakout over data centers is just another fracking backlash we need to ignore
item.description: America's important fracking victory offers a blueprint for AI data center builders facing 70% public opposition and major Chinese competition.
item.content:encoded:
The future of America as a high-tech superpower is at a tipping point.

The latest Fox poll shows 70% of Americans now oppose building new data centers in their communities, even though they are crucial to our future as a high-tech economy. Another report shows that 40% of new data centers have been delayed or canceled in 2026 — news that’s deeply welcome to our opponents in the artificial intelligence (AI) and tech race, the Communist Chinese Party.

Data centers have become an electoral issue for the midterms, even in a red state like Texas where Republican Gov. Greg Abbott has announced a construction moratorium. It’s probably the only thing he has in common with ultra-liberal Democrat Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York: a willingness to hit the pause button on data centers.

FROM NEW YORK TO TEXAS, STATES SHOULD RESPECT LOCAL CONTROL ON DATA CENTERS

This backlash comes despite the fact that every policymaker knows that data centers are needed to power our future economy, from AI to the Internet of Things and the cloud, and that the only real beneficiary of a moratorium will be China. Still, the public remains unconvinced, especially when it faces a zoning proposal to build a data center half a mile from its backyard.

This all sounds discouraging, but we’ve been here before. Just a decade ago, the advent of large-scale fracking, or horizontal drilling, for oil and gas faced a similar frenzy of opposition. If today’s anti-data center forces have strong support from communist China (which has been linked to more than 200 accounts on X, promoting data center misinformation) then it was Russian President Vladimir Putin’s Russian media that amplified the anti-fracking movement here and in Europe.

FOX NEWS POLL: COOL YOUR SERVERS! VOTERS REJECT DATA CENTERS

It got so bad that fracking became a flashpoint in the culture wars, with left-wing celebrities like Jane Fonda, Matt Damon and Mark Ruffalo organizing protests and blockades, resulting in bans on fracking in several states.

Yet, in the end, the fearmongers lost and the energy companies won, as did America’s strategic and economic interests. Today, thanks to fracking, America is the world’s No. 1 oil and gas producer. That’s why hostilities with Iran haven’t caused a panic at the pump. A new report by the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston says without America’s current oil and gas independence, the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz would have cut the U.S. employment rate by nearly 2%.

How the energy companies turned the public around on fracking offers powerful lessons for today’s AI executives and power companies on data centers.

KEVIN O'LEARY WARNS CHINA IS WINNING THE AI RACE BECAUSE U.S. STATES ARE SLOWING DATA CENTER PRODUCTION

First, fracking companies understood that all politics with environmental issues like this, is local. This isn’t a war you can macro-manage from the boardroom or Washington. Instead, it’s a series of wars that have to be fought state by state, district by district, even neighborhood by neighborhood.

This means partnering with local businesses and local governments, to talk about how building a new data center expands jobs and opportunities for everyone, not just AI or tech companies. It also means seeking out places that will welcome a new data center for the same reasons, and using them as examples of how data centers can coexist with traditional communities and values.

CHINESE BOT FARM CAUGHT RED-HANDED TRYING TO INFLUENCE HEATED AI DATA CENTER DEBATE

Second, it means partnering with responsible environmental and citizen associations to emphasize how data center builders will be staying within agreed-upon safety and cost guidelines, such as President Donald Trump’s insistence that they come with their own power supply so as not to raise electricity rates. This partnership can work to dispel the myths being spread by the opposition.

One of those myths that nearly stopped fracking was that it polluted the water supply. Companies were able to prove that fracking didn’t affect the water supply except where the water table was already low- and where engineers wouldn’t want to sink a well, anyway.

‘BACKWARDS AND POOR’: TRUMP ISSUES DIRE WARNING TO COMMUNITIES BLOCKING CRITICAL TECHNOLOGY

Anti-data center fanatics spread similar falsehoods about data centers using up water, when in fact your average golf course consumes more. Likewise, companies can emphasize that technical and safety improvements take place every year. The data centers built five years ago will look like technological dinosaurs compared to the ones that are coming.

Third, don’t let up on the focus of what happens if we don’t. Fracking executives were able to remind people of what energy dependence looked like, with long gas lines and soaring prices. We can remind average Americans of the gains China will make, and the advantages we lose, if Beijing wins the data center wars. Do you really want the country that gave us COVID-19 deciding the future of AI?

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Finally, people need to realize new data centers aren’t just about growing AI. They’re essential to modern life, as the number of devices we use requires more and more power. The average U.S. household uses between 17 and 21 internet-connected devices, compared to only two or three devices in 2010. All that connectivity makes increasing demands the future grid won’t be able to match without new data centers.

America, and Americans, won the battle over fracking 10 years ago. They can do it again with data centers today.

FLORIDA MAN WHO ALLEGEDLY LURED WOMEN WITH DATING APP COULD HAVE MORE VICTIMS: AUTHORITIES

item.title: College football's first full Saturday is here and it's a celebration of America at its best
item.description: The Wisconsin Badgers and college football traditions unite millions of Americans at tailgates with cold beer, brats and burgers every Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
Ladies and gentlemen, greatness has finally arrived.

Today marks a moment that serves as a yearly reminder that America is the greatest country on the planet and no other country comes close:

The first full slate of college football on a beautiful Saturday in the USA.

THESE ONCE-ANNUAL COLLEGE RIVALRIES USED TO DEFINE COLLEGE FOOTBALL AND NEED TO MAKE A COMEBACK ASAP

There are a lot of great things to celebrate about the glorious country we all call home. Freedom, the Second Amendment, the greatest military in the history of the world, gorgeous nature from coast to coast, cheap domestic light beer and other examples that would take me a month to list.

However, college football holds a unique place in this country. It represents something we should all hold near and dear to our hearts:

American exceptionalism.

It’s the one sport that brings people together in a way no other sport does. Yes, the NFL and other sports leagues unite fans, but not in the way college football does.

This sport is rooted in traditions that span generations and have endured through two world wars, economic booms, depressions and social strife. Most importantly, it binds family and friends.

Stop and think about it for a second. Why do you cheer for your college football team? The answer is almost always the same: You either attended the university or your parents or grandparents raised you to be a fan of that team.

URBAN MEYER, COLIN COWHERD SAY BIG TEN VENUES AND FANS HAVE CAUGHT UP AND 'BYPASSED THE SEC'

In my case, it's both. I was raised in a house whose emotions were directly tied to the success of the Wisconsin Badgers, and I later (barely) graduated from the University of Wisconsin. You couldn't get me to cheer for a different team at gunpoint, and I make no apologies for setting my schedule around Wisconsin football.

You think the communists in North Korea have this kind of freedom? Not a chance.

This day is about celebrating the fact America is better than every other place on this planet, and you'll find us dead before you find us regretting it or apologizing for it. It's never going to happen.

Today, millions of Americans will gather at tailgates, bars and at homes with one goal and one goal only:

Supporting their favorite college football team.

It almost makes me a bit misty-eyed even thinking about it.

While much of the rest of the world eats bad food and settles for watching soccer or whatever they watch in other countries, Americans will celebrate our country at its finest with college football, cold beer, hot brats and burgers and time with friends and family. I wouldn’t have it any other way. Raise a toast and enjoy an epic first full Saturday of college football.

P.S.: I am fully ready to be emotionally destroyed by the Badgers again.

item.title: MLB player spent the week becoming a US citizen, and then did something incredible in his first game back
item.description: Eugenio Suarez missed two Cincinnati Reds games to pass the US naturalization test, then returned to a surprise walkup song and a mammoth home run.
item.content:encoded:
It may be another lost season for the Cincinnati Reds, but that doesn't mean everyone has thrown in the towel.

In fact, some players are using this final month of the season to really focus on the little details of baseball: getting that average up, stealing a few more bags, hitting for power, and, of course, becoming a citizen of this great country.

That's right. Becoming a United States citizen — otherwise known as the best test you'll ever pass.

OPINION: SPORTS IS ONE OF AMERICA'S GREATEST TRADITIONS AND A POWERFUL FORCE THAT UNITES US

Reds slugger Eugenio Suarez did just that earlier this week, when he missed two games to take the U.S. naturalization test. The 35-year-old passed with flying colors, and then was greeted with a surprise when he returned to the ballpark Friday night.

Suarez's teammates changed his walkup song to "God Bless The USA." The veteran slugger then promptly hit a mammoth home run in the third inning.

Patriot.

Incredible. God, I love this country. Between Eugenio Suarez becoming a US citizen launching a home run in his first game back, and the return of college football today, who has it better than us right now?

Nobody. Imagine being European today. Or Canadian. Imagine being anywhere else on the planet besides America.

Sounds horrific. Sounds like a nightmare.

Eugenio Suarez made his feelings about the country perfectly clear this week. And by the way, missing two games isn't an easy thing to do — especially after the month Suarez just had.

MLB UMPIRE BILL MILLER MISSES EVERY ABS CHALLENGE IN REDS COMEBACK WIN OVER CUBS

The Venezuelan hit six home runs and drove in 20 runs in August while also posting an .852 OPS. Not bad for a 35-year-old who was, inexplicably, placed on waivers by the Reds earlier in the month.

Nobody scooped him up, so the Reds threw him back in the lineup and he responded by being the best hitter on the team for a few weeks.

That's the American way! The land of second chances.

On the season, Suarez is hitting just .207, but he's third on the team with 21 home runs. He has 346 career home runs over a 13-year MLB career that's seen him play for Detroit, Seattle, Arizona, and two stints with the Reds.

God bless the USA.

What a country.

item.title: Prince Harry, Meghan Markle accused of seeking ‘best of both worlds’ with UK move: expert
item.description: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's U.K. return mirrors the "half-in half-out" arrangement Queen Elizabeth rejected, a royal expert says.
item.content:encoded:
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have returned to the United Kingdom with their two children, but royal experts say the move may be less about a permanent homecoming and more about securing the "best of both worlds."

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex — who are reportedly looking for a home in Britain — are expected to maintain their ties to Montecito, California, while keeping their businesses based in the United States. 

Royal commentator Kinsey Schofield told Fox News Digital that the reported arrangement appears to give the couple access to Britain and the royal family while allowing them to maintain their independent lives in the U.S.

"I suspect they want the best of both worlds — access to Britain, proximity to the monarchy and the credibility that comes with Harry’s royal identity, while maintaining the freedom and commercial opportunities they associate with life outside the U.K.," Schofield said.

PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON FACE 'SUSSEX CIRCUS' AS PRINCE GEORGE PREPARES FOR ETON: EXPERT

Schofield said the Sussexes’ reported plans resemble the "half-in, half-out" role that Queen Elizabeth II rejected when Harry and Meghan stepped back from royal duties in 2020.

MEGHAN MARKLE’S UK RETURN POSES PALACE CONTROL ‘NIGHTMARE,’ EXPERT WARNS

While the couple has reportedly vowed to avoid making public comments or releasing photos that could overshadow Prince George's start at Eton this month, Schofield said the Sussexes’ broader U.K. plans raise questions about whether they are truly returning to Britain for good or simply testing the waters.

"Harry and Meghan never do what they say or say what they mean," she said. "One year ago, Harry told us the U.K. was not safe enough to bring his wife and children. Now someone is briefing the Daily Mail that Harry has a 15-year plan in the U.K. Alternatively, we’re briefed this could be temporary."

"I would describe it as a trial run rather than a definitive homecoming," Schofield added.

Harry and Meghan relocated to California in 2020 after stepping back as working members of the royal family. Since then, they have released various projects, including a Netflix docuseries and Harry’s memoir, "Spare," and have pursued a series of entertainment and business ventures outside the monarchy.

However, their return to Britain has raised questions about their motives.

Royal commentator Richard Fitzwilliams said Harry and Meghan have increasingly presented themselves as an "international" power couple, rather than tying themselves to either the U.K. or the U.S.

PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE'S UK RETURN SIGNALS ‘SPECTACULAR DEFEAT’ AS ROYAL EXPERTS WARN OF WILLIAM SHOWDOWN

"They reportedly see themselves as ‘international citizens,’" Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital. "They claim that their balance of business activities and trips abroad over the last six years is a success."

WATCH: PRINCE HARRY BELIEVED ROYAL FAMILY COULD HAVE ALLOWED A ‘HYBRID’ ROLE: AUTHOR

"Rather than planting one flag, the Sussexes appear to be keeping several doors open," Schofield added.

Helena Chard, a British broadcaster and photographer, also said Harry and Meghan are "keeping their options open."

"Things haven’t gone to plan for various reasons, but one thing’s for sure: They need to keep relevant," Chard told Fox News Digital. "Cue travel to the U.K., be seen with the British Royal Family and push for state-funded armed police protection."

Chard said enrolling the children in a British school could benefit the family while also helping Harry pursue the security arrangements he has sought since stepping back as a working royal.

"Like a dog with a bone, Harry will fight for everything he believes his family deserves," Chard said.

The experts also questioned whether Harry and Meghan are equally invested in making Britain a permanent home.

"Harry has much more at stake emotionally," Schofield said. "Returning gives him an opportunity to reconnect with his country, his family, old friends and a version of his identity that he walked away from six years ago."

"For Meghan, Britain carries different associations," she continued. "She has repeatedly described her royal experience as deeply unhappy, so I think it is reasonable to question whether she could ever feel the same enthusiasm Harry might feel about putting down permanent roots."

"Harry may see Britain as coming home. Meghan may see Britain as somewhere useful to spend part of the year," Schofield said. "Those are two very different emotional investments."

item.title: Father who rejected Democrats' sympathy rips 'ignorance' after emotional Capitol Hill hearing
item.description: Marcus Coleman rejected Democratic lawmakers' sympathy at a Capitol Hill hearing, saying none ever reached out after his daughter's life-changing crash.
item.content:encoded:
A father rejected Democratic lawmakers' expressions of sympathy on Capitol Hill this week, accusing them of only showing concern when the cameras are rolling after his daughter was left permanently disabled in a car crash allegedly caused by an illegal immigrant.

"I reject your guys' sympathy, to be honest with you. There's no way you guys are sorry," Marcus Coleman told lawmakers Tuesday.

Coleman criticized Democratic lawmakers for what he called their "ignorance" during a follow-up interview Thursday, telling Fox News' Trace Gallagher that he struggled to make them understand his position.

"Talking with the Democrat representatives, I mean, the language they speak is ignorance, and it's hard for me to translate what I'm trying to say to them," he said. "I can explain it all day, I just can't understand it for them."

ANGEL DADS FACE ANOTHER FATHER'S DAY WITHOUT CHILDREN KILLED BY ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS: 'SHE SHOULD BE GRADUATING'

His remarks come after a heated CNN discussion about crimes involving illegal immigrants, during which podcast host Leigh McGowan described the discussion as "exhausting."

Coleman told Gallagher about his own "exhausting" experience caring for his 7-year-old daughter, Dalilah, after she was critically injured in 2024 when an 18-wheeler traveling at about 60 mph slammed into the car she was riding in.

The Department of Homeland Security identified the truck driver as Partap Singh, an illegal immigrant from India who had obtained a commercial driver's license in California. DHS said Singh was driving at an unsafe speed and failed to stop for traffic and a construction zone before the crash.

"I work on maybe about four hours of sleep every night, primarily taking care of my daughter during the daytime, trying to work at nighttime and squeeze everything in, so I'm exhausted," Coleman said.

ANGEL MOM WARNS DEMOCRATS 'WE'RE NOT GOING TO STOP' AFTER EMOTIONAL HOUSE HEARING ON SANCTUARY POLICIES

Coleman said his daily responsibilities have made it difficult to accept what he views as indifference from lawmakers.

During Tuesday's hearing, he accused Democratic lawmakers of offering sympathy inside the committee room while failing to reach out to him privately.

"Not one of you guys have ever called me. Not one of you guys ever reached out to me," Coleman told them. "You guys do it right here while you guys are grandstanding on top of your soapbox."

"This is when you guys care," he continued. "Right here inside this room is the only time you guys cared."

At a previous sanctuary cities hearing, Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., questioned why the committee was revisiting the issue.

"Unfortunately, this hearing is — it's the fourth time in this committee that we've had a hearing on sanctuary cities. The fourth time," Jayapal said. "And there's many other things that we could be doing other than this."

Coleman said his advocacy will continue despite the demands already placed on him at home, saying his daughter's condition is a reminder of what he believes is at stake in the country's immigration debate.

"There's no remedy with open borders at all," he said.

"Leaving your door unlocked at nighttime, you're not gonna sleep safe. Leaving the borders open at nighttime, we're not going to be safe. My daughter is the proof. There's hundreds, if not thousands, of victims right now behind illegal aliens."

Fox News' Stephen Sorace contributed to this report.

item.title: Trump’s Pentagon shake-up revives a presidential power play with a long history
item.description: Dan Driscoll's exit as Army secretary intensifies debate over whether Trump's Pentagon overhaul strengthens or destabilizes military leadership.
item.content:encoded:
Dan Driscoll’s departure as Army secretary has brought new scrutiny to the Trump administration’s sweeping changes at the Pentagon, with Democrats and some Republicans warning that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s approach is creating instability among the military’s top leaders.

But the president replacing senior military leaders is nothing new. Presidents from Abraham Lincoln to Harry Truman have removed commanders when they lost confidence in their leadership, disagreed over strategy or wanted a different direction.

What stands out about the current moment is the pace of the turnover — and the debate over whether the administration’s changes are putting the military on a stronger footing or creating leadership gaps along the way.

COMMANDING GENERAL OF THE US ARMY IN EUROPEAN AND AFRICAN THEATER IS UNEXPECTEDLY STEPPING DOWN

North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis said Hegseth is "creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks" while ranking Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee Jack Reed of Rhode Island said, "Hegseth is cultivating a culture where dissent is punished, and competence is secondary to personal allegiance."

Under Trump's second term, at least 20 military leaders have departed over a combination of clashes, including over Hegseth's leadership, military strategy, as well as disagreements over DEI, according to a CBS report.

Parnell told Fox News Digital that the Pentagon is "unified behind" Hegseth’s vision.

"Secretary Hegseth has been a transformative leader for the Department of War and, at President Trump’s direction, has ushered in a new era of Peace Through Strength. Standards and merit are back, our arsenal is stronger than ever before, and morale and recruitment across every service are at all-time highs," added Parnell. "Secretary Hegseth has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way."

Presidents dating back to Abraham Lincoln have removed senior military leaders when they believed a change in personnel was necessary — a longstanding feature of civilian control of the military, not a new invention of the current administration.

Then-President Barrack Obama accepted Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel resignation in 2014 after the president concluded that new Pentagon leadership was needed amid disagreements over the administration’s strategy against ISIS, Syria policy and the management of the Defense Department.

PENTAGON FIRES BACK AFTER MARK KELLY ACCUSES PETE HEGSETH OF TARGETING WOMEN AND BLACK MILITARY OFFICERS

Reports at the time indicated the departure was a forced resignation.

Following Hagel's departure, Obama said the former Defense Secretary had "guided the department through this transition" and that it was "an appropriate time for him to complete his service." He praised Hagel for helping modernize the military’s strategy and meet Obama's concern for longterm threats such as China’s rise and Russian aggression.

Harry Truman removed five-star Army general and one of the most prominent U.S. commanders of World War II Douglas MacArthur.

The two men clashed over the Korean War with Truman wanting to avoid spreading conflict to China while MacArthur advocated for the opposite.

One early example came during the Civil War, when Abraham Lincoln removed Gen. George McClellan as commander of the Army of the Potomac after growing frustrated with his cautious approach to fighting Gen. Robert E. Lee. Lincoln later removed Ambrose Burnside after the Union’s defeat at Fredericksburg and replaced him with Joseph Hooker.

RENEWED PATRIOTISM AND CAREER OPPORTUNITIES FUEL ARMY'S BIGGEST RECRUITING SURGE IN YEARS

Trump named Adam Telle as acting secretary of the Army Thursday, calling him "a Great Patriot, who is respected by all" and saying he would assume the role immediately after Driscoll’s resignation.

Telle previously was the Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works. 

Driscoll's exit comes after reportedly butting heads with Secretary of War Pete Hegseth over concerns with the administration about the Army’s transformation and readiness, including his belief that Hegseth had hindered those efforts.

Vice President Vance said Thursday Driscoll was a "very good friend" of his and was a "great secretary of the Army."

Vance acknowledged that he agreed with Hegseth, that there is a need to "have a culture shift at the Department of War."

US ARMY HITS 2026 RECRUITING GOALS FOUR MONTHS EARLY, PETE HEGSETH ANNOUNCES AT WEST POINT COMMENCEMENT

"Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more," White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement.

"The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War," she added.

Trumps entered his first administration with the message of peace through strength seeking to reinvent global perception of America while also modernizing the military such as creating the U.S. Space Force.

During his first term, Trump had two Senate-confirmed defense secretaries, including Jim Mattis, who resigned in 2018 after Trump announced plans to withdraw U.S. troops from Syria, and Mark Esper, whom Trump fired in 2020 after disagreements that included the military’s role in responding to domestic unrest.

"Changes in civilian leadership at the military-service level aren’t unusual. During President Trump’s first administration alone, the Army had two Senate-confirmed secretaries, Mark Esper and Ryan McCarthy, while Robert Speer and McCarthy also served as acting secretaries during leadership transitions," a senior Pentagon official told Fox News Digital.

"There’s a reason the law is structured this way," the official added. "The Department of the Army operates under the authority, direction, and control of the Secretary of Defense, and the Secretary of the Army is specifically responsible for ensuring Army policy is consistent with the President’s and Defense Secretary’s national-security policies and that their decisions and instructions are implemented effectively and on time."

Trump came back during his second term with an aggressive approach to rebuilding the American military, tightening fitness requirements, axing DEI policies, overhauling weapons acquisition, building up recruitment and refocusing the force on combat readiness and lethality.

item.title: MARK HALPERIN: Social media damaged a generation. Are we about to let AI do the same?
item.description: The social media crisis offers a cautionary lesson as AI companies build chatbot products that could intimately interact with children unchecked.
item.content:encoded:
Imagine: two hundred aliens land on Earth, with thousands and thousands more of them expected in looming, unstoppable waves.

And imagine, too, that we know some of the aliens are here to help us, to make our planet better, smarter, and more efficient. But we also know that some of the aliens are here to do us harm, perhaps injure us irreparably. What we don’t know is this: which aliens will be good to us, and which will be malevolent?

That is the situation with AI.

But it is more complicated than that.

PARENTS PUSH CONGRESS TO ACT ON KIDS' ONLINE SAFETY AFTER JURIES FIND META AND YOUTUBE LIABLE FOR HARM

Because the good aliens and the bad aliens aren’t necessarily different aliens. The same technology that can help discover a cure for cancer, give a low-income kid access to a world-class tutor, make government more efficient, and produce extraordinary new wealth also can deceive, manipulate, displace, addict, and destroy. The alien who comes bearing gifts in the morning might be the one who burns down the village at night.

And yet for the multitudes of op-eds and think pieces, the anxious parent text chains and furtive bot-synthesized office memos, the accelerating quotidian reliance on AI for driving directions, recipes, fun facts, and how-tos, we aren’t discussing AI with the frequency and intensity it warrants.

We are merely watching, transfixed and paralyzed; or turning away and scurrying back to landlines and paperback books; or playing along, sinking into the lazy comfort of an easy answer. An algorithmic echo of Ray Bradbury’s 1948 short story, "Mars is Heaven."

REP. TED LIEU: AI IS ALREADY TOO POWERFUL. WE NEED A KILL SWITCH BEFORE DISASTER STRIKES

There is little doubt that AI will be the next leap forward in human advancement, akin to the printing press, the Industrial Revolution, penicillin, and the internet. But we are not having the urgent, necessary conversations about what it all means.

China, meanwhile, is all in on AI, investigating its most sinister uses, learning its gifts and powers, leveraging it, weaponizing it. In the United States, however, the topic of AI veers shambolically from flippant Matrix memes to end-of-days-style apocalyptic panic, to tepid comparisons with old-school Google.

WHEN AI TESTS CAUSE DAMAGE, WE NEED STRONGER SAFEGUARDS AND REAL ACCOUNTABILITY

The implications of AI are so vast, so incomprehensible, that it is unclear which entities are equipped to wrangle it, or at least enforce some regulations, whether it is the White House or Congress, the two branches united, or state-by-state legislation. Additionally, AI is changing so quickly, and government moves so slowly, that by the time any measures are passed, the technology that prompted the hearings might be several generations old.

One can look at the rise of social media to see a clear, cautionary analogy.

NEW MEXICO SEEKS MASSIVE PENALTY FROM META AFTER JURY FOUND TECH GIANT LIABLE FOR ENDANGERING CHILDREN

What began as an innocuous way to share life updates, family photos, and dog videos grew enormous and toxic, changing the way people, especially children and teens, process information. Changing their hobbies and passions and brain chemistry. Changing the way they make friends, view themselves, and interact with the world. Social media has transformed the way we get news and connect with people, but belatedly, has induced a scramble to scale back the more malignant elements of its influence, especially on the young.

The great lesson of social media isn’t simply that we failed to regulate it. It is that we waited to see what would happen.

SEN. BERNIE SANDERS: YES, WE MUST HIT THE PAUSE BUTTON ON AI BEFORE IT IS TOO LATE

We let hundreds of millions of people use it, let the companies optimize it, let children become consumed by it, and then, years later, began accumulating the evidence of what it had done. Only after the patient got sick did we start looking for the right medicine.

Meta recently took a significant step and acknowledged its contribution to the crisis, following a massive nationwide lawsuit accusing the company of deliberately designing Facebook and Instagram to be addictive to young people, along with charges that the company was intrusive and unethical with its data collection.

UK TO BAN TIKTOK, YOUTUBE, OTHER SOCIAL MEDIA APPS FOR CHILDREN UNDER 16, STARMER SAYS

In addition to paying out as much as $18 billion in damages, Meta promised to make major changes to how children and teenagers may access and use their platforms. Meta further called upon its industry competitors, YouTube and TikTok, to enact similar alterations.

For years, millions of parents, regardless of political affiliation, have pleaded for this sort of reform.

AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU

Mark Zuckerberg and the other innovators who built the social media revolution can rightly argue that they did not know, at least in the very beginning, what they were creating or the impact it would have. Nobody in a Harvard dorm room in 2004 had a body of evidence showing what Facebook would do to the sleep patterns, self-esteem, attention spans, friendships, politics, and mental health of the children coming of age behind them.

But the people who are now building and selling AI have no such excuse.

They have the entire social media experience sitting right in front of them. They know what happens when extraordinary technology meets the human desire for attention, companionship, affirmation, stimulation, and convenience. They apprehend the commercial incentive to keep the customer engaged for another minute, another hour, another year.

And AI presents a problem that social media never did.

MAJORITY OF YOUNG ADULTS SAY THEY ARE 'MORE CONCERNED THAN EXCITED' ABOUT AI: PEW RESEARCH

Facebook can influence your child. Instagram can make your child feel inadequate. TikTok can keep your child staring at a screen until two in the morning.

AI can become your child’s friend.

Or tutor, therapist, confidant, or adviser. Or romantic interest. Or some combination of all of these relationships.

It can know what your child is afraid of. Who your child has a crush on. What your child hates about their body. What is going wrong at home. What your child hasn’t told a parent, a teacher, a sibling, or a best friend. A generation of children could grow up pouring the most intimate details of their lives into machines owned and operated by corporations.

Think about that for a moment.

The danger isn’t just what AI tells our children. It is what our children tell AI.

So far, most AI executives, with a technological power that makes the social media platforms look like humble floppy disks from Radio Shack, have not shown much interest in doing the right thing.

But they should. They should take a look around at their communities, their own children, and consider the brave new world they are poised to create.

There are obvious places to begin. Parents should know when and how their children are using AI. Children should always know when they are dealing with a machine rather than a human being. There should be serious limits on the collection and retention of children’s most personal information. AI companionship for minors deserves scrutiny of an entirely different order than asking a chatbot who won the Battle of Gettysburg. There should be limits on how aggressively these products can be designed to keep a child engaged, and how they can be used, particularly late at night and without a parent’s knowledge.

The major AI companies could agree on a set of basic rules for children, an AI Geneva Convention of sorts. Not because these companies have suddenly become charities, and not because competition has ceased to matter. As Meta urged TikTok and YouTube, if everybody plays by the same rules, nobody is forced to choose between responsible behavior and market share.

The standard Silicon Valley response to regulation has been that anything that slows American technology hands the future to China. There is truth in that. The United States cannot unilaterally disarm in the AI race while Beijing charges forward.

But protecting American children is not unilateral disarmament.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

We can race China to build the smartest AI without racing China to see who can most effectively manipulate a 12-year-old. We can lead the world in artificial intelligence without surrendering an entire generation to it.

For AI products designed specifically to interact intimately and repeatedly with children, perhaps the companies first should have to demonstrate that reasonable protections exist. The consequences of being too careful are only that a child waits a little longer for some new feature. The consequences of being too cavalier are potentially disastrous.

There is a still deeper question that doesn’t fit neatly into legislation or parental controls.

What happens to childhood when a child never has to be bored?

Or lonely. Or confused. Or stumped. Or forced to figure something out without assistance. What happens when every question receives an immediate answer, every insecurity an immediate reassurance, every empty hour an available companion?

Those things sound like problems technology should solve.

But boredom, uncertainty, frustration, loneliness, and even failure have been part of growing up since there have been children. These human challenges help produce imagination, independence, resilience, judgment, and the ability to exist inside your own head.

The strangest danger of AI may turn out not to be that it does terrible things for our children.

It may be that it does wonderful things for them, all the time, so easily and so completely that we discover too late that AI has eliminated essential parts of how children learn to become adults.

There surely will be casualties of the AI revolution. But our children should not be among them.
